reason: 'metallic sheen/lustre' on perigynia, fruits, leaves and stems means the surface reflects a lot of light, i.e. it is shiny. PATO_0002277 iridescent needs the colour to change with the viewing angle, which these statements don't say.
FLOPO reticulate is defined as forming or being marked by a network, explicitly including veins. It suits sepals, fruits and valves, which PATO_0001972 reticulodromous (leaf venation only) does not.
Same meaning as the existing rule for 'low' (C184): a short plant. Every statement is about the whole plant.

'Leaves in a rosette' and 'plant ± rosette' mean rosulate, and FLOPO rosulate already has 'rosette' as a related synonym. 'Rosette leaves' used as a noun is the bearer rosette leaf (PO_0000014), not a quality.
Trichotomous means forking into three, the counterpart of the existing rule dichotomous = bifurcated. PATO tripartite is 'divided into three branches' and has the exact synonym trifurcate.

Paleaceous means chaffy: thin, dry and scale-like, as said of pappus elements and bracts. The exception is 'receptacle paleaceous' (Asteraceae), which means the receptacle bears paleae; that use should be entity_presence of flower bract (PO_0009034, synonym chaff).

'Homogeneous endosperm' is the standard opposite of ruminate endosperm. Its uses for oil bodies, cells and costae (meaning not segmented, or of one cell type) have no clear single quality and should stay unannotated.
Veins or areas 'not raised' do not stand out from the surface. PATO_0001369 raised is defined only for colonies, and the existing rule maps 'elevated' to prominent.

'Broadest at, above or below the middle' places the widest point along the length. This is the axis behind ovate, elliptic and obovate, plus a position (base, middle, apex), so it needs a pattern rather than a term. The earlier rejection of bare 'broadest' still stands.

The colour green (PATO_0000320) is a firm value. 'Paler' is a comparison with another part or surface (usually the adaxial one), so it belongs in the relation pattern; without that second part only the green is kept (see rejected 'paler', C241).

Stilt roots are shoot-borne roots that arise above ground from the stem and grow down into the soil, which is exactly PO prop root. PO also lists 'stilt root' as a narrow synonym of its parent, shoot-borne root (PO_0000042).
'Bare' leaves out what is missing: leaves on stems and branches, pappus on cypsela tips, hairs elsewhere. Like 'covered' (C240), the meaning depends on a part that isn't named.
A prefix cut off from a range such as 'bi- to tripinnate' or 'bi- to tristratose'. The parser should complete it (bipinnate, bistratose); on its own it means nothing.

label: callose
definition: A texture quality inhering in a bearer by virtue of the bearer's bearing hard, thickened and often raised areas (calli).
reason: Common in descriptions of orchid lips, legume petals and leaf margins. The noun 'callus' was rejected as a generic part (and PO_0005052 plant callus is wound tissue), so the hardened state needs a quality. It sits beside FLOPO tuberculate.

label: obpyriform
definition: A convex 3-D shape quality inhering in a bearer by virtue of the bearer's being pear-shaped with the broad end distal, tapering towards the point of attachment.
reason: The reverse of PATO_0005002 pear shaped, whose definition fixes the narrow end at the top. So obpyriform cannot be its child and becomes a sibling, as obovoid was handled.
A flange is a thin, flattened rim projecting from the body (stipule margins, spore equator, fruit apex). That matches PATO winged's 'thin, flattened extensions that project from its main body'.
Stiped means borne on a stipe, i.e. stipitate. Statements like 'stipe 0–4 mm' are measurements of the bearer stalk (rule C264).
Floriferous means bearing flowers. Fractions such as 'stems 1/4–1/2 floriferous' give how much of the stem carries flowers and belong in RDF; 'more floriferous' is a comparison and adds nothing firm.

Mamillae are low, rounded, nipple-like bumps, which fits 'small rounded protuberances'. Bryologists separate mamillose (the cell bulges) from papillose (solid thickening), so it should not go to papillose. 'Operculum mamillate' is a nipple-tipped shape and fits less well.
Two shape values run together: ovate (FLOPO:0991024) and orbicular (PATO_0001934), the latter approximate per docs/odp/01-approximate-value.md. It is a continuum between them, not a new shape.
Negation of PATO winged, which exists; the earlier rejection of 'winged' was only as a bearer.

label: viviparous
definition: A structural quality inhering in a seed or reproductive structure by virtue of its germinating or producing a plantlet while still attached to the parent plant.
reason: A real botanical trait (mangroves, viviparous grasses and spikelets) with no term in PATO. The parent follows the precedent of dehiscent (FLOPO:0991149), a behaviour at maturity placed under structure; the parent is the uncertain part.
An abundance or frequency modifier ('gemmae frequent', 'hairs frequent to dense'), not a quality of the part. The parser should record the part as present and keep the modifier in RDF.

label: panduriform
definition: A 2-D shape quality inhering in a bearer by virtue of the bearer's outline being fiddle-shaped: broader towards the apex and contracted by a concave indentation on each side below the middle.
reason: A standard leaf, petal and bract shape with no PATO term. It sits beside the FLOPO 2-D shapes ovate and obcordate, and differs from FLOPO lyrate (pinnatifid with a large terminal lobe).
Bristle-tipped is aristate, and the existing rule C207 maps aristate to 'awn present'; PO awn has the synonyms arista and bristle. Same rule, for consistency.
'Pappus copious', 'albumen copious' and 'sap copious' mean present in large amount or number. PATO increased amount also has the synonym increased number.

Imperfect flowers are unisexual, and FLOPO unisexual already lists 'imperfect' as a synonym. Moss uses ('endostome trellis imperfect', meaning incompletely formed) are a different sense and stay unannotated.
Eroded margins and lobes are irregularly toothed, as if gnawed, which is PATO erose. 'Pyrene sides eroded' (pitted surfaces) is a weaker fit.

label: semi-woody
definition: A texture quality inhering in a bearer by virtue of the bearer's being only partly hardened by lignification, woody at the base or in parts and herbaceous elsewhere.
reason: A common habit and stem quality (Fr. semi-ligneux). PATO has no woody term, and PATO_0002352 herbaceous is about die-back, so it goes under texture beside FLOPO corky.
Polished seeds, fruits and stipes are smooth and shiny; PATO glistening has the exact synonyms glossy and shiny. 'Polished cloth' is a fragment, not a quality.
